e.etymology: An African-American name of the 1970s made by adding the La- prefix to Kisha, a spelling of Keisha.
A spelling of Diane, the French form of Diana, the Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon, whose name goes back to a root meaning divine or heavenly.
A spelling of Karen, the Danish short form of Katherine, from Greek Aikaterine. The traditional meaning pure comes from a later link with Greek katharos.
e.note: Sounds the same as Karen, now slang for an entitled, complaining woman.

assoc.t: sounds the same as Karen, slang for an entitled complainer

e.etymology: A spelling of Earl, the English title of nobility, from Old English eorl, nobleman or warrior. The final e comes from the surname.
A phonetic spelling of Lisa, a short form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath.
The feminine form of Alfred, from Old English Aelfraed, which joins aelf (elf) and raed (counsel).
A French elaboration of Flora and Flore, from Latin flos, flower.
An American name built on Marquis or Mark with the Spanish diminutive ending -ita, used mostly in African-American families and most popular in the 1980s.
The garden flower, one of the flower names in fashion around 1900. The word comes from French pensee, thought, because the bloom was seen as a symbol of remembrance.
e.note: Pansy is also a dated insult for a timid or effeminate man.

assoc.t: pansy, an insult for a timid or effeminate man

e.etymology: A spelling of Claude, the French form of Claudius, a Roman family name from Latin claudus, lame.
A spelling of Shelly or Shelley, an English place name and surname from Old English words for a ledge and a clearing. It also serves as a pet form of Michelle, Rochelle and Shirley.
An American elaboration of Gay or Gayle with a feminine -a, in the pattern of Kayla and Twyla. It sounds like one pronunciation of the word gala.
Usually a short form of longer names such as Aretha and Margaretha.
Usually explained as a variant of Wanda that follows its Polish pronunciation. In mid-century America it also sat beside Vonnie, Rhonda and Yvonne.
A spelling that covers two names: Carroll, the Irish surname from O Cearbhaill, descendant of Cearbhall, given to boys, and Carol, the short form of Caroline, given to girls.
A phonetic spelling of Deirdre, the tragic heroine of Irish legend known as Deirdre of the Sorrows. The meaning of the Old Irish name is uncertain.
A spelling of Felicia, from Latin felicia, happy things or happy times, built on felix, fortunate. Felicia is the feminine counterpart of Felix.

assoc.t: Bye, Felicia, a dismissive catchphrase from the film Friday

e.note: Bye, Felicia, a line from the 1995 film Friday, is a common way to wave someone off.

e.etymology: A mid-century name close to Deanna and Diane, often written DeAnn as if Dee plus Ann. Some families use it as a feminine form of Dean.
A spelling of Kathy, the pet form of Katherine and Kathleen, from Greek Aikaterine. The traditional meaning pure comes from a later link with Greek katharos.
A spelling of Bernice, from Greek Berenike, the Macedonian form of Pherenike, bringer of victory. A Bernice appears in the Book of Acts.

e.note: Oma is the everyday German and Dutch word for grandma.

e.etymology: A spelling of Debbie, the pet form of Deborah, from Hebrew devorah, bee. Deborah is the prophetess and judge of the Book of Judges.
namesakes: Debby Boone (singer, You Light Up My Life)

e.etymology: A spelling of Karen, the Danish short form of Katherine, from Greek Aikaterine. The traditional meaning pure comes from a later link with Greek katharos.
e.note: Sounds the same as Karen, now slang for an entitled, complaining woman.

assoc.t: sounds the same as Karen, slang for an entitled complainer

e.etymology: A spelling of Patty. Today Patty is a pet form of Patricia, from Latin patricius, noble; in the 1800s, when Pattie peaked, it was mostly a pet form of Martha, by way of Matty.

assoc.t: York Peppermint Pattie, the chocolate mint candy

e.etymology: An African-American name of the 1970s that adds the La- prefix to Shonda, a feminine form of Shawn.
A spelling of Patricia with the second i dropped. Patricia is the feminine of Patrick, from Latin patricius, a patrician or member of the Roman nobility.
A spelling of Doris, Greek for a woman of the Dorian people. In myth Doris is a sea goddess, the mother of the fifty Nereids.
An English surname used as a first name for both sexes. For girls in the 1940s it overlapped with Cheryl and Sheryl, which sound the same.
A mid-century American name that reads as Lois with the De- prefix and overlaps with Deloris, a spelling of Dolores.
An early 1900s American spelling of Rita, the Spanish and Italian short form of Margarita and Margherita, from Greek margarites, pearl.
An American variant of Dorothea, from Greek doron (gift) and theos (god), the same elements as Theodora in reverse order.
A spelling of Misty, the English adjective used as a name. Misty spread after the jazz standard Misty (1954) and the 1971 film Play Misty for Me.
